c0618: Zoning check before signing: restaurant use, Type I hood route, electrical service and seats
c0621: Ask the city planning (zoning) office whether the zoning allows a restaurant with flat-tops and fryers, whether the space can take a Type I hood with a duct up to the roof, what electrical service it has, whether gas reaches it and what occupancy load it allows. Then ask the fire marshal in writing what the hood and fire suppression requirements are. With no exhaust path to the roof there are no flat-tops and no fryers.
c0622: Decide your format before signing the lease: counter service with take-out and delivery, delivery-only, or a burger bar with servers
c0624: Counter service with an order counter, take-out and delivery (this plan: 44 seats in about 1,700 sq ft, or 158 sq m); delivery-only (a ghost kitchen) in 450-650 sq ft (40-60 sq m); a gourmet burger bar with servers in 1,300-1,600 sq ft (120-150 sq m), with tips on top; or a burger truck (see the Food Truck Business Plan Kit). Each one needs a different space, investment and margin.
c0625: Decide before signing: buy ground beef (or pre-portioned balls) or grind in-house
c0626: If you buy it already ground (or in pre-portioned balls), the supplier is responsible for the grinding: ask for its establishment number, lot and pack date on every delivery. If you grind in-house, the grinder and its space go into the kitchen plan, and a house-grind log (lots, establishment numbers, time of each grind and each cleaning) is good practice: ask your health department what it expects.
c0627: Decide before signing: frozen fries or fresh-cut
c0628: The plan uses frozen fries (3/8" crinkle). Fresh-cut means peeling, cutting, soaking or blanching, space, water and kitchen hours: the kit's calculator tells you up to what labor cost it pays off.
c0629: Choose your entity (LLC or S corp with your CPA) and get your EIN
c0632: The projections use an effective income tax rate (see "0. Assumptions"). A pass-through LLC or S corp pays no income tax at the entity level and the tax lands on your personal return. Compare the options with your CPA using the figures of the plan.
c0633: Business license + sales tax permit (state and city)
c0636: Apply for the general business license with your city or county and for the sales tax permit with your state's tax agency before you open. Some states tax to-go food differently: ask your CPA.
c0641: State plus local approval, with timelines that vary. Apply early: approval is never guaranteed. Make the lease contingent on it if you can, and add liquor liability to your insurance.
c0648: Bring the full financial plan, with the month-by-month cash flow. Also ask for a lease or financing offer on the flat-tops, the fryers and the refrigeration.
c0652: General liability, product liability, liquor liability (beer), property with fire and refrigeration breakdown cover, and workers' comp. Tell the broker you run gas flat-tops and fryers: it changes the premium and the terms.
c0658: Second-generation restaurant space of about 1,700 sq ft (158 sq m) with a route for the Type I hood
c0660: Room for the open kitchen with two flat-tops and the fryers, an order counter with a self-order kiosk, 44 seats (tables and a window counter), restrooms (one ADA-accessible) and a to-go packing and driver pickup area by the door. A neighborhood with nightlife or a campus area.
c0664: Gas flat-tops and fryers, refrigeration, the makeup air of the hood and HVAC add up. Ask the utility whether gas reaches the space and at what capacity. A service upgrade or a new gas connection takes time: ask for the lead time and the cost.
c0667: A dedicated, continuous, sealed duct to the roof, through a shaft or the facade, with the landlord's approval if it crosses common areas. Two flat-tops and three fryers always need a Type I hood: ask the fire marshal in writing.
c0669: The plan counts two months of rent before opening and two months of security deposit. Ask for a free-rent period while the build-out, the duct and the gas lines are done.
c0673: It should say restaurant use and allow the kitchen build-out, the duct to the roof and the gas lines. Ask your attorney to review the hood rights and the beer & wine license contingency.
c0677: Layout of the kitchen, order counter and dining room, power, gas, occupancy load, ventilation, accessibility and the duct to the roof. Ask your city what its hood and mechanical requirements are.
c0687: Type I hood installed under a mechanical permit, with UL 300 fire suppression and makeup air, and signed off by the fire marshal. The flat-tops and the fryers throw off a lot of grease: ask the installer for the duct cleaning records.
c0688: Exhaust fan and grease filters over the whole hot line, connected to the dedicated duct
c0691: Hood with exhaust fan and grease filters that covers both flat-tops and all three fryers, connected to the dedicated duct. Ask the installer for the airflow rating and the filter cleaning plan.
c0692: Gas lines by a licensed plumber or gas fitter, with permit and inspection
c0695: Pressure test and start-up of each gas appliance by the licensed contractor, with permit and inspection by the local authority. Keep the paperwork: your insurer and the fire marshal ask for it.
c0696: Build-out of the kitchen, order counter and dining room with smooth, cleanable surfaces
c0698: Washable walls, slip-resistant flooring (the grease of the flat-tops reaches the floor), cleanable ceilings, hands-free hand sinks in the kitchen, restrooms (one ADA-accessible) and soundproofing if you have neighbors
c0700: Hot and cold water in the kitchen, drains with a grease interceptor (the flat-tops and the fryers send a lot of grease down; the county sizes it at plan review) and HVAC for the dining room: with the flat-tops on, the open kitchen heats the room
c0701: To-go packing and driver pickup area by the door
c0702: A table with the burger boxes, fry cups, sauce cups and bags, the ticket printer and the marketplace tablets, so drivers never cross the dining room or enter the kitchen
c0703: Final electrical, gas and building inspections → certificate of occupancy
c0706: The final electrical inspection, the gas inspection and the final building inspection. Keep every sign-off: the certificate of occupancy and the health department's pre-opening inspection ask for them.
c0712: The health permit comes from your county or city health department, after the plan review (Food Code 8-201.11). Selling beef balls to other businesses is a different activity and may need another license: ask your health department.
c0713: Written food safety plan: raw ground beef at 41 °F or below, stored below ready-to-eat food
c0716: Keep raw ground beef at 41 °F (5 °C) or below, stored below ready-to-eat food and separate by species (Food Code 3-501.16, 3-302.11). Salt the smash on the flat-top, not ahead of time. Put a thermometer and a log on the walk-in.
c0717: If you grind: keep a house-grind log (lots, establishment numbers, time of each grind and each cleaning)
c0720: This kit does not claim that a grinding log is mandatory for a restaurant: FSIS requires grinding records (9 CFR 320.1(b)(4)) of retail stores and official establishments that grind raw beef, so ask your health department what it expects from you. A house-grind log is good practice. Work out each day's pounds with the kit's calculator and grind in small batches.
c0721: Keep supplier establishment numbers, lots and pack dates for every beef delivery
c0723: Write down the supplier's establishment number, the lot and the pack date of every delivery, and file the data sheet (blend and lean/fat ratio; the case works with 80/20). Reject beef that arrives above 41 °F (5 °C).
c0724: Ground beef only from approved suppliers with data sheets (no dry-aged program in this plan)
c0726: Buy from suppliers your health department accepts (inspected, with their establishment number) and with the data sheet of the blend (chuck, brisket, short rib). This plan has no dry-aged beef in the burger: a plan you will show an inspector does not need it.
c0727: Cook every smash to 155 °F for 17 seconds; probe one per batch
c0728: The Food Code (3-401.11(A)(2)) asks for ground beef to reach 155 °F (68 °C) for 17 seconds (or 145 °F (63 °C) for 3 minutes, 150 °F (66 °C) for 1 minute, or 158 °F (70 °C) instantly); your state adopts its own edition. The kit's rule: every smash to at least 155 °F for 17 seconds, checked with a thin-tip probe on one per batch, because color and crust do not certify the temperature. Log it. If you ever offer burgers cooked to order, add the consumer advisory (3-603.11).
c0729: Receiving log (beef at 41 °F or below) and separate raw-meat tools and trays
c0731: Measure and log the temperature of every delivery and reject beef that arrives above 41 °F (5 °C). Spatulas, tongs, boards and trays for raw beef stay separate from those for cooked burgers and ready-to-eat food, with hand washing between one and the other.
c0732: Consumer advisory on the menu, website and marketplace listings if you offer cooked-to-order
c0734: Only if you offer burgers cooked to order (at the guest's request): a disclosure ("hamburgers (can be cooked to order)" or an asterisk) plus the reminder "Consuming raw or undercooked meats, poultry, seafood, shellfish, or eggs may increase your risk of foodborne illness" (Food Code 3-603.11), on the menu, the website and every marketplace listing. Never offer them on the kids' menu or to highly susceptible populations (3-801.11). The case serves everything cooked through and needs no advisory.
c0735: Fries: fry at 350-355 °F to a golden color; California: ask your attorney about the Prop 65 warning
c0736: There is no federal acrylamide limit for restaurants. Fry to a golden color, not dark brown, at 350-355 °F (177-179 °C), skim the oil often and keep a color guide for the fries and the toasted buns in view of the staff. In California, ask your attorney about the Prop 65 warning for fried potatoes.
c0737: Filter fryers nightly and change the oil by TPM (no federal limit); used oil to a licensed renderer
c0738: There is no federal limit on total polar materials (TPM). Filter every night, add nothing to the oil but oil, and change it by your TPM reading (test strips or a tester) or the manufacturer's guidance. Log each change. Used oil goes to a licensed renderer, never down the drain or back into the kitchen.
c0739: Hot holding at 135 °F or above (cheese sauce, chili); cool and reheat per Food Code
c0740: Hot holding at 135 °F (57 °C) or above. Cooling: from 135 °F to 70 °F (21 °C) within 2 hours and to 41 °F (5 °C) within 4 more hours; reheat to 165 °F (74 °C) for 15 seconds (Food Code 3-501.14, 3-403.11).
c0741: Cut produce and sauces on the make line at 41 °F or below, date-marked (7 days)
c0742: Cut lettuce, tomato and onion and the sauces, ready to build, go at 41 °F (5 °C) or below: in the refrigerated prep unit, in covered pans, and cut fresh each day. Date-mark ready-to-eat food held more than 24 hours (7 days maximum at 41 °F: Food Code 3-501.17).
c0743: Traceability and logs: lots, dates and temperatures
c0744: Lot, supplier, establishment number and pack date of the beef; lot of the buns, cheese, fries and sauces; temperatures of the walk-in, the prep unit and the probe check; and oil changes
c0745: Recipe cards for every burger with its major allergens
c0746: Ounces of ball, bun, cheese, sauces and sides of each item, with its major allergens: the bun (wheat; milk, egg and soy depending on the recipe; sesame if it has seeds), the American cheese (milk), the sauces (egg in the mayo), the shakes (milk; peanuts or tree nuts in the mix-ins) and the breaded chicken (wheat, egg and milk). Mustard is not a major allergen in the US. With the kit's calculator, the cost of each one.
c0751: Use the higher of the federal minimum wage ($7.25 an hour) and your state or local minimum for your lowest pay rate, and enter it in the "0. Assumptions" sheet. Everyone is paid hourly as a W-2 employee; this plan has no servers and no tip credit, and the tip jar belongs to the team.
c0752: Hire the lead grill cook BEFORE the build-out
c0753: The flat-top is the bottleneck of the service: let whoever will run it try the layout and weigh in on the make line before you close the kitchen. If only the owner can run the flat-top, one absence closes the line.
c0761: Open 7 days, 11:00 a.m. to 10:00 p.m. (11:00 p.m. on Friday and Saturday), with the kitchen opening at 8:30 a.m. On Friday and Saturday nights you need about six people: two on the flat-tops, one on the fryers and the make line, one at the counter, one packing and one at the expo.
c0765: CFPM + food handler cards, with ground beef and fryer safety
c0766: Have a Certified Food Protection Manager where your state requires one (Food Code 2-102.12), and food handler cards where your state or county asks for them. Add documented in-house training: hygiene, ground beef temperatures, the probe check, fryer oil, major allergens and cross-contact.
c0767: Line training: ounces per ball, the smash and the build
c0768: Everyone portions, smashes and builds the same way: weigh 10 balls from each person and correct them. A ball that runs heavy is food cost that never shows up in the recipe costing.
c0771: Part of your duty to provide a safe workplace (OSHA): burns from the flat-tops and the fryers, slips on grease, cuts and heavy lifting
c0777: Allergen matrix (9 major in the US) with the bun, sauces, cheese, shakes and breaded items
c0778: One row per item and one column per allergen, with what is forgotten most: the sesame on the seeded bun, the egg in the mayo and the sauces, the wheat in the breaded chicken, and the milk in the cheese and the shakes. Update it every time a supplier or a recipe changes.
c0779: Never promise "gluten-free" with a wheat bun, a shared fryer and a shared flat-top (21 CFR 101.91)
c0781: A "gluten-free" claim has to meet 21 CFR 101.91 (under 20 ppm of gluten in the finished food). With a wheat bun toasted on the same flat-top and a fryer that shares oil with the breaded items, disclose the wheat allergen and the cross-contact risk. If you offer a separate bun that its maker labels gluten-free, serve it without promising anything for the finished burger.
c0784: Short menu of about 14 items and the combo
c0786: Six smash burgers (single, double, triple, with bacon, Oklahoma-style and the house burger), a crispy chicken sandwich, a veggie burger, classic and loaded fries, a shake, a dessert, the double combo with fries and a drink, and the combo for two: the 14 rows of the costing in the calculator. On top of that, three sauces, soft drinks, beer and water. A menu of 12 burgers and 6 sauces fills the walk-in with buns and ingredients that get thrown out.
c0787: Cost per burger and per combo by channel (calculator)
c0789: Use the Smash Burger Patty, Fries & Costing Calculator in the kit: the cost of each item, always against the price excl. sales tax, and the margin in the dining room, for take-out and on the marketplaces. Even with the higher marketplace price, the combo leaves about a quarter less margin there than in the dining room.
c0790: Sales tax on the menu: one rate in the plan
c0792: The example uses a single sales tax rate (8%). Some states tax to-go food differently from dine-in, and alcohol can carry its own rate: ask your CPA, then set the POS and each marketplace up the same way.
c0793: Check your state's rules for to-go food and combos
c0794: The combo and the shake: check how your state taxes a bundled meal and a shake, because some states treat to-go food, dairy drinks or combos differently. If your state asks for it, break the combo down by component on the receipt.
c0796: Some cities and states restrict polystyrene foam, plastic straws and utensils unless the customer asks for them, so check your local ordinances before you order boxes. Ask your supplier which of your wrappers, burger boxes and fry cups comply.
c0797: Two beef suppliers with data sheets and establishment numbers
c0798: With a single supplier, one bad week leaves you without a menu. Ask each one for the data sheet of the blend (chuck, brisket, short rib), the lean/fat ratio (the case works with 80/20), the establishment number and pack date on every delivery, the delivery temperature and the price in writing: the plan estimates them.
c0799: Bun and fries suppliers with data sheets and allergens
c0800: The potato bun with its allergen list (wheat; milk, egg, soy and sesame depending on the recipe) and the frozen fries with their data sheet (cut, coating and allergens) and the manufacturer's frying instructions
c0804: Calculate the margin of the combo on the marketplace with its commission, the menu markup and the packaging; pickup at the restaurant pays no commission: push it with the website, the kiosk and the phone. A smash burger travels worse than it looks: the crust softens, so use vented containers for the fries and send them out last.
c0805: Allergens before ordering and hot food out fast (consumer advisory in the listing if you offer cooked-to-order)
c0807: Show the major allergens in the online menu before the guest orders, on your site and on every marketplace listing (and the consumer advisory if you offer cooked-to-order). Pack the order in boxes and bags that hold the heat, and send it out fast.
c0811: Search the USPTO database first to check the name is not taken in your class (restaurant services). Real photos and videos of the flat-top and the burgers; a website with the menu, the allergens, the hours, pickup ordering and the privacy policy of each channel.
c0812: Google Business Profile, Yelp, Instagram and TikTok and peak dates (National Burger Month, Super Bowl Sunday, March Madness)
c0813: Lunch and dinner hours, photos of the flat-top and a reply to every review. On the calendar: Super Bowl Sunday and March Madness, National Burger Month and graduations in May, and the summer.
c0820: The plan starts in January and the ramp-up runs from January to April; February is the slowest month, with January and November behind it. That is why working capital counts. If you open in another month, rotate the seasonality row of the "12-Month Cash Flow" tab.
c0822: Cleaning schedule for the flat-tops, fryers and make line
c0823: The flat-tops and their scrapers, the fryers and their filtering, the hood filters, the refrigerated prep unit, the walk-in and the to-go packing area, each with its log
c0826: Several practice services to fine-tune the ounces per ball, the flat-top timing, the build and the packing of orders before you open
c0829: Walk-in, prep unit, the probe check on the smashes, the fryer oil temperature and the cleaning sheet; fix any deviation before you serve
c0832: Delivery records with the beef's establishment number and pack date, temperatures, probe checks, oil changes, allergen sheets, traceability, cleaning, training and pest control
c0833: Weigh 10 balls, measure cook loss and fries portions, and recalculate (calculator)
c0835: Weigh 10 balls before and after the flat-top (the cook loss), count the portions of fries that come out of each pound and take the averages to the kit's calculator; then compare your actual food cost (food purchases ÷ food sales for the month) with the plan's.
c0836: Log TPM readings and every oil change
c0838: With test strips or a tester, or by the interval your food safety plan sets; note how many portions each vat gives you and take the figure to the calculator. Used oil goes to the licensed renderer.
c0839: Hood and duct cleaning schedule per NFPA 96, flat-tops, gas and refrigeration
c0842: Hood and duct cleaning on the NFPA 96 schedule (quarterly with heavy grease, twice a year if moderate: ask the fire marshal), service of the flat-tops and the gas lines, and the refrigeration technician for the walk-in and the prep unit
c0845: In ice water or as the manufacturer says, and logged: an uncalibrated probe says a ball is done when it is not
c0850: Covers per day, average check, food and labor against the Excel P&L; re-cost the menu whenever the price of beef changes
c0852: January opens the ramp-up and February is the slowest month: look at each month's balance before a big payment
